newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SPH to post lacklustre growth - analysts.
newsitem.headline: SPH to post lacklustre growth - analysts.

text.p: Media group Singapore Press Holdings was expected to post lacklustre profit growth for the past financial year as a slowing economy hit advertising and steep newsprint prices affected earnings, market analysts said.

Analysts told Reuters on Thursday they projected a mild net profit growth of between 2.0 percent and 8.0 percent for the year ended August 31, 1996. SPH had been recording double-digit growth until fiscal 1995 when it was hit by high newsprint prices.
"I'm projecting a net profit of Singapore $318 million (US$225.5 million), a two percent growth," said Michael Sia, analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

SPH, which controls all of Singapore's daily newspapers in all languages, is expected to announce full-year results in early November. It recorded a 6.3 percent rise in net profit to Singapore $310.98 million in the year ended August 31, 1995.
The latest Estimate Directory put SPH's fiscal 1996 consensus net profit at S$334.7 million, a rise of 7.6 percent.

Sia also projected a 2.0 percent decline in advertising volume, while most other analysts saw flat volume growth. This was after advertising volume growth had slumped from 16 percent in 1993/94 to 6.0 percent in 1994/95, analysts said.
Analysts said revenue growth from newspaper operations would be positive, lifted by two advertising rate hikes SPH imposed in August 1995 and in January 1996.
The company derives 95 percent of its revenue and about 87 percent of its pretax profit from newspaper sales, circulation and advertising, analysts said.
Singapore's slower economic growth, which became more apparent after the first half this year, has further eroded SPH's advertising demand.
"The company didn't do as well as expected in the first half before the economic slowdown. (Since then) the slowdown has dragged volume growth even more," said Sia.
"Classified recruitment ads have been falling consistently from the second half," said Paul Heng, analyst at Fraser Securities.
"The property side has also come down after the anti-speculation measures...it all adds up," Heng said.
The government in May introduced measures to curb speculation in the property market, resulting in property prices and the number of real estate transactions falling.
High newsprint prices have also eaten into SPH's profitability, but the situation should improve from fiscal 1997.

One analyst from a foreign broking house said newsprint prices averaged US$945 per tonne for SPH in fiscal 1996, against US$721 per tonne the previous year. She saw newsprint prices for SPH easing to US$635 per tonne in fiscal 1997.

Analysts said SPH would aim to raise its margins in 1997 with more colour advertising after new presses become fully operational. A colour advertisement can command a premium of as much as 50 percent over a black and white, they said.
But they added that the extent of the impact of the new presses on earnings was still unclear.
"How much better earnings will be in fiscal 1997 really depends on demand. If there is no slowdown in demand, SPH could return to double-digit growth," said Heng.
